item.title: QFactorial and Monash University Secure A$1.12 Million ($$758.6K USD) Australian Government Grant for Quantum Logistics Optimization
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article highlights a rare government‑backed effort to push hybrid quantum‑classical methods into a real‑world supply‑chain problem, marking one of the first large‑scale logistics pilots that couples QFactorial’s routing software with IBM Quantum and AWS cloud resources. By targeting freight and last‑mile delivery—domains where classical combinatorial solvers already strain under massive data volumes—the project could demonstrate tangible speedups or cost reductions that validate quantum advantage beyond academic benchmarks. It also signals growing policy momentum in Australia to nurture critical‑technology ecosystems, echoing similar initiatives in Europe and the United States. However, the 15‑month timeline underscores that practical quantum benefits will still hinge on hardware improvements and seamless integration with existing enterprise workflows.

QFactorial and Monash University have received a A$1.12 million Australian government grant to develop a hybrid quantum-classical optimization solver for freight and last-mile delivery. The 15-month project aims to advance QFactorial's routing and fleet-utilization platform. This initiative, part of the Critical Technologies Challenge Program, involves a consortium including IBM Quantum, AWS, and Fujitsu, and seeks to overcome limitations of classical solvers in large-scale logistics. item.title: Quantum XChange Phio TX Becomes First Post-Quantum Cryptographic Management Platform to Earn EUCC Certification
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article highlights a milestone for post‑quantum security: Quantum XChange’s Phio TX becomes the first PQC management platform to secure EUCC certification, complementing its existing U.S. FIPS validation. The approval clears a major regulatory hurdle for European enterprises that need certified tools to deploy lattice‑based algorithms and integrate quantum key distribution while meeting data‑sovereignty requirements. It also signals that the ecosystem of vetted, standards‑compliant PQC solutions is finally catching up with the accelerating timeline for migration away from classical cryptography.

Quantum XChange's Phio TX cryptographic management software (version 4.5.6) is the first post-quantum cryptography (PQC) management platform to achieve EUCC certification, adding to its existing U.S. FIPS validation. This certification, valid until November 9, 2031, allows for the secure deployment of post-quantum algorithms and quantum key distribution interfaces within the European Union, simplifying procurement and supporting data sovereignty. item.title: JIJ Launches SQOA Solver in IBM Quantum Functions Catalog to Tackle Combinatorial Optimization Beyond Qubit Counts
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article is noteworthy because JIJ’s SQOA Solver shows a practical route to bypass the current qubit‑count bottleneck by compressing problem variables and offloading much of the heavy lifting to classical subspace diagonalization, something few quantum‑software offerings provide today. By demonstrating 384‑node MaxCut and 200‑node MIS on IBM hardware, it builds on recent hybrid approaches such as QAOA‑enhanced classical preprocessing and signals that large‑scale combinatorial optimization may become feasible before fault‑tolerant machines arrive. The result is a more accessible toolkit for enterprises seeking quantum advantage on near‑term devices, though the performance still hinges on the quality of the encoding and the underlying hardware noise levels.

JIJ Inc. has launched its SQOA Solver in the IBM Quantum Functions Catalog, allowing users to tackle complex optimization problems with more variables than available qubits. This solver utilizes a novel approach that combines variable-compression encoding and classical subspace diagonalization, eliminating the need for iterative quantum hardware optimization. It has demonstrated success in solving large-scale problems like 384-node MaxCut and 200-node Maximum Independent Set on IBM Quantum hardware. item.title: Atom Computing Finalizes $100 Million U.S. Department of Commerce R&D Agreement for Fault-Tolerant Quantum Systems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article marks a rare infusion of large‑scale federal money into neutral‑atom quantum hardware, signaling that the U.S. government now sees Atom Computing’s approach as a viable path toward fault‑tolerant qubits. By moving logical‑qubit architectures from laboratory prototypes to repeatable production, the $100 million grant could accelerate the timeline for utility‑scale machines and give the neutral‑atom platform a foothold alongside superconducting and trapped‑ion competitors. The deal also positions Atom as the sole Stage‑C participant in DARPA’s Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, opening up to an additional $300 million of funding that may help bridge the gap between experimental error correction and commercial workloads. However, scaling neutral‑atom arrays to millions of qubits will still require breakthroughs in laser control and packaging before true fault tolerance can be demonstrated at scale.

Atom Computing has finalized a $100 million R&D agreement with the U.S. Department of Commerce to accelerate the commercialization of fault-tolerant, utility-scale quantum systems. This funding will support hardware engineering and manufacturing scale-up at their Boulder, Colorado operations, moving logical-qubit architectures into repeatable commercial production. The company is also the only neutral-atom vendor in Stage C of the DARPA Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, representing up to $300 million in potential federal funding. item.title: German Aerospace Center (DLR) Researchers Demonstrate Low-Cost Benchmarked-Noise Error Mitigation Across 100-Qubit IBM and IQM Processors
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the German Aerospace Center has turned error mitigation into a truly scalable tool by combining randomized benchmarking with zero‑noise extrapolation, Pauli twirling, dynamical decoupling and TREX to improve expectation‑value accuracy without adding extra measurement shots. Demonstrating the technique on 100‑qubit IBM and IQM devices proves it works at the scale where many near‑term applications—such as quantum chemistry or optimization—are beginning to run, addressing a long‑standing bottleneck of noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) hardware. By keeping the overhead low, bnZNE could become the default “software‑only” fix for developers seeking higher fidelity results before full error correction arrives, though its performance will still depend on device‑specific noise characteristics and calibration stability.

Researchers at the German Aerospace Center (DLR) have developed an improved quantum error mitigation protocol, randomized benchmarked-noise zero-noise extrapolation (bnZNE). This method enhances expectation-value accuracy without increasing measurement shot budgets, validated on 100-qubit IBM and IQM processors. The bnZNE protocol incorporates Pauli twirling, dynamical decoupling, and twirled readout error extinction (TREX), outperforming standard zero-noise extrapolation across various benchmarks. item.title: QodeX Quantum, NVIDIA, RTX BBN, and U.S. Navy Researchers Forecast Unstructured PDEs on 52-Qubit IBM Hardware
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that a hybrid quantum‑reservoir network can solve unstructured nonlinear PDEs on a real 52‑qubit device, pushing quantum simulations well beyond the coherence‑time limits that have traditionally constrained circuit depth. By beating classical baselines on fluid‑dynamics benchmarks, the work signals that near‑term hardware combined with clever algorithmic structures may already deliver practical advantages for engineering problems. It also dovetails with recent efforts to harness noisy intermediate‑scale quantum (NISQ) processors for scientific computing, suggesting a viable pathway toward quantum‑accelerated CFD and related fields. Readers should note, however, that the results rely on extensive classical post‑processing and are currently limited to modest mesh sizes, so scaling will require further advances in both hardware fidelity and algorithmic efficiency.

A research team from QodeX Quantum, NVIDIA, RTX BBN, and U.S. Navy researchers successfully demonstrated gradient-free forecasting of nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) on unstructured engineering meshes using up to 52 qubits on an IBM Quantum Heron r3 processor. Their hybrid quantum reservoir network (QRN) achieved significant error reduction compared to classical baselines and executed circuits far longer than typical qubit coherence times. This advancement, detailed in a technical preprint on arXiv, showcases a novel approach to quantum computation for complex fluid dynamics. item.title: Rigetti Computing Integrates Quantum Elements Constellation Platform into Error Correction Pipeline
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows Rigetti’s adoption of Quantum Elements’ Constellation simulator into its quantum error‑correction workflow, giving the company a way to predict single‑ and two‑qubit gate fidelity on its 36‑ and 108‑qubit superconducting chips before hardware runs. By modeling device physics early, Rigetti can iterate hardware designs faster and move toward fault‑tolerant architectures, echoing similar software‑in‑the‑loop strategies pursued by IBM and Google as the field scales beyond a hundred qubits. The integration provides a quantitative handle on error mechanisms that is essential for scaling, though its accuracy still hinges on well‑calibrated noise models and will need experimental validation on real processors.

Rigetti Computing has integrated Quantum Elements' Constellation simulation environment into its quantum error correction (QEC) workflow. This allows Rigetti to model processor behavior and predict system performance, including single and two-qubit gate fidelity, on their 36-qubit and 108-qubit quantum processing units. This integration helps Rigetti characterize device physics and optimize hardware designs before running on actual quantum processing units, aiding in the scaling of superconducting quantum processors towards fault tolerance. Q-CTRL, a quantum infrastructure software provider, has raised $290 million in Series C funding led by Salesforce Ventures, valuing the company at over $1 billion. This funding will be used to expand its AI-driven control software and scale global commercial deployments in various sectors. The company's software products, Fire Opal, Boulder Opal, and Ironstone Opal, focus on quantum computer noise suppression, calibration automation, and GPS-denied quantum magnetic navigation. item.title: Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM Cross 12,000-Atom Barrier in Heterogeneous Quantum-Classical Drug Binding Simulations
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first heterogeneous quantum‑classical simulation of a protein‑ligand complex with more than 12 000 atoms, showing that near‑term quantum processors can already contribute useful electronic‑structure detail to drug‑binding calculations when paired with classical supercomputers. The new Embedded Wavefunction formalism and TrimSQD algorithm extend the size frontier beyond previous ~100‑atom quantum chemistry benchmarks, building on recent advances in hybrid quantum methods such as QM/MM and variational embedding. While the approach still relies on a large classical workload and error‑mitigated 156‑qubit hardware, it provides a concrete pathway toward quantum advantage in pharmaceutical modeling as devices scale.

A collaboration between Cleveland Clinic, RIKEN, and IBM Quantum has achieved the largest heterogeneous quantum-classical (HQC) electronic-structure calculation to date, simulating protein-ligand complexes exceeding 12,000 atoms. This research utilized 156-qubit IBM Heron r2 processors and leadership supercomputers to significantly advance molecular size and fragment energy accuracy in drug binding simulations. The team developed an Embedded Wavefunction (EWF) formalism and TrimSQD to efficiently handle these complex calculations, leading to the first HQC protein-ligand binding energy prediction. item.title: Ensemble phase transitions in measurement-unitary hybrid quantum circuits
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article uncovers a new kind of “ensemble phase transition” that occurs in hybrid circuits where unitary gates are punctuated by projective measurements, showing that the statistical properties of both trajectory and projected state ensembles change abruptly at the measurement‑induced purification point even though their average states stay maximally mixed. By linking these non‑analytic ensemble shifts to the well‑studied entanglement‑purification transition, the work provides a concrete mechanism for how measurements can break deep ergodicity and generate higher‑order unitary designs—insights that could sharpen diagnostics of quantum hardware and inform error‑mitigation strategies. The results also highlight stark differences between Haar‑random and Clifford circuits, suggesting new routes to probe non‑stabilizer resources essential for universal quantum computation. Readers should care because understanding these ensemble dynamics may enable more reliable control of measurement‑driven protocols in near‑term devices.

The universal properties of state ensembles generated by quantum dynamics provide a refined lens into Hilbert-space ergodicity and deep thermalisation, or lack thereof. We investigate deep-ergodicity breaking transitions of an ancillary qubit entangled with a system undergoing dynamics via hybrid quantum circuits, where unitary evolution is interspersed with projective measurements. Specifically, we analyse the statistical properties of two distinct state ensembles: the trajectory ensemble (TE) conditioned on the measurement outcomes of the hybrid circuit, and the projected ensemble (PE) generated by further projective measurements of the system at the final temporal boundary. We find that both ensembles undergo non-analytic changes -- ensemble phase transitions -- at the critical point of the measurement-induced purification transition, despite their first moments remaining completely maximally mixed and blind to the transition. For Haar-random circuits, the TE transitions from a trivial identity ensemble to the uniform Haar ensemble, while the PE transitions from the Haar ensemble to a trivial singleton pure state. In Clifford circuits, absence of non-stabiliserness limits the PE to a $1$-design, while the TE forms a $k$-design for $k \leq 3$. We demonstrate that these genuine ensemble transitions offer a clear physical mechanism for the measurement-induced entanglement or purification transitions, illustrating how the capacity to ergodically steer a quantum subsystem shifts from the temporal boundary measurements in the mixed phase to the bulk trajectory measurements in the pure phase.

item.title: A deployed four-city entanglement-based QKD network with real-time key delivery, benchmarked against finite-key security bounds
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates the first operational, entanglement‑based quantum‑key‑distribution network that spans four cities without any trusted repeaters, showing that a fully meshed topology can be built from passive wavelength routing using a new matrix formalism. By delivering keys in real time through the ETSI GS QKD 014 stack and benchmarking against finite‑key security bounds, the work moves beyond laboratory coincidence counts to a practical, standards‑compatible service with measurable secret‑bit rates of up to 13.5 bits s⁻¹ over 109 km. The authors also identify that swapping the current detect‑and‑discard approach for full error correction could boost finite‑key rates by more than a factor of four, pointing toward scalable, high‑performance quantum cryptography for national fiber infrastructures.

Quantum key distribution (QKD) generates shared secret keys whose security rests on the laws of physics rather than on computational assumptions. We report the entanglement-based segment of the Slovak national quantum communication infrastructure, connecting four cities in western Slovakia over deployed telecommunication fiber. Polarization-entangled photons generated at a central node are passively routed by wavelength to form a trusted-node-free, fully meshed sub-network of three cities, with the fourth connected through the central node and all links operated simultaneously. We also introduce a matrix formalism for passive wavelength routing that enables the algorithmic construction of uniquely and fully connected topologies. Unlike most previous demonstrations, which estimate key rates from raw coincidences, all rates reported here are obtained after the complete post-processing chain, with keys delivered in real time via ETSI GS QKD 014. With partial non-local chromatic dispersion compensation, we obtain 13.5 bit/s over 109 km, and 4.3 bit/s over 32.1 dB of accumulated loss between two cities without a direct fiber link. Benchmarking against finite-key security bounds shows that the implemented heuristic privacy amplification can exceed the finite-key bound, and that replacing detect-and-discard with error correction would increase the finite-key rate by a factor of 4.1-6.6, and yield a positive finite-key rate on the 142.9 km link where the implemented scheme yields none.

item.title: Implementation of a 1D Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD under finite-size parameter estimation
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article reports the first fully integrated experimental demonstration of a one‑dimensional Gaussian‑modulated CV‑QKD system using independent lasers and a local‑local oscillator, achieving a privacy‑amplified key rate of 1.421 Mbit/s (asymptotic) and 0.364 Mbit/s when finite‑size effects are included over 12 km of standard fiber. By simplifying the modulation to a single quadrature while still delivering megabit‑per‑second rates, it addresses long‑standing hardware complexity concerns and brings continuous‑variable QKD closer to practical telecom deployment. The results also highlight that finite‑size parameter estimation remains a bottleneck, underscoring the need for larger data blocks or more efficient reconciliation to reach commercial‑grade performance.

Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) is a promising technology for quantum-secure communications, offering high secret-key rates and straightforward integration with coherent optical communication systems. Conventional Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD encodes information in both optical-field quadratures, increasing requirements for state preparation, modulation, and calibration, while potentially introducing additional preparation imperfections. Unidimensional (1D) Gaussian modulation offers a simpler alternative by encoding information in only one quadrature, while the conjugate quadrature constrains the protocol's security. However, an integrated experimental 1D implementation combining independent-laser coherent reception with practical reconciliation, finite-size parameter estimation, and privacy amplification remains challenging. Here, we experimentally demonstrate a 1D Gaussian-modulated CV-QKD system over 12~km of standard single-mode fiber using a local local oscillator (LLO) architecture with independent lasers and an integrated offline classical post-processing chain. The implementation includes coherent detection, digital signal processing, information reconciliation, parameter estimation, physicality-constrained security analysis, and privacy amplification. The 1D system achieves a privacy-amplified rate of $1.421$~Mbit/s under the asymptotic security treatment and $0.364$~Mbit/s under the finite-size scenario. These results establish an experimental baseline for the performance--complexity trade-off associated with unidimensional Gaussian modulation and provide an experimental basis for developing lower-complexity CV-QKD transmitters.

item.title: Programming Quantum Circuit Parameters with Large Language Models
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that a frozen, general‑purpose large language model can directly suggest full parameter sets for variational quantum circuits, offering a shortcut to the costly classical optimization loop that underpins most VQE workflows. The study finds the shortcut works best when the target Hamiltonian exhibits recognizable physical or mathematical structure—such as molecular or parent‑Hamiltonian problems—while it struggles on generic random instances and gains little from iterative feedback. By highlighting both the promise of AI‑driven circuit initialization for structured quantum chemistry tasks and its current limits, the work helps steer future hybrid approaches toward problems where problem‑specific patterns can be leveraged.

Large language models (LLMs) have recently demonstrated the ability to generate parameters for variational quantum circuits without conventional optimization. However, the conditions under which this approach is effective remain unclear. Here, we investigate a frozen, general-purpose LLM that generates complete circuit parameter vectors from symbolic circuit and Hamiltonian descriptions, with optional iterative energy feedback. We evaluate the approach on general random Hamiltonians, structured parent Hamiltonians, and molecular systems. For general Hamiltonians, LLM-generated parameters exhibit larger energy errors than conventional Adam optimization, while additional feedback generally provides limited improvement. In contrast, for structured Hamiltonians, the LLM can generate promising low-energy parameter configurations, suggesting that identifiable physical and mathematical structure facilitates parameter inference. We also show that direct LLM predictions of minimum energies can violate the Hamiltonian spectral lower bound, whereas generated circuit parameters allow independent evaluation of physically realizable energy expectation values. Finally, we investigate blind circuit interpretation and find that the LLM can predict measurement outcomes even when it fails to identify the underlying quantum algorithm. These findings highlight the role of problem structure, the limitations of iterative LLM optimization, and the importance of independently verifiable predictions in quantum parameter programming.

item.title: Explicit Absolutely Maximally Entangled states in dimensions twice a prime power
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article delivers the first explicit families of absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states in local dimensions that are twice an odd prime power, closing a long‑standing gap in multipartite entanglement constructions and completing the nine‑party AME classification for all integer dimensions ≥ 3. By coupling qubits with higher‑dimensional q‑level systems, the authors obtain scalable AME(N, 2q) states that can be directly translated into optimal quantum error‑correcting codes and secret‑sharing schemes, a development that dovetails with recent advances in high‑dimensional quantum networking and holographic code design. The work also highlights an exponential growth requirement on q for larger N, underscoring both the power of the new construction and the remaining challenge of finding more resource‑efficient AME states.

Absolutely maximally entangled (AME) states are pure multipartite states with maximally mixed reductions on every set of at most half the parties. We construct explicit families in local dimension $2q$, twice an odd prime power $q$, using an established coupling of qubits and $q$-level systems. The $q$-level states remove interference between branches, so the qubit states need maximally mixed reductions only on average. This gives AME$(9,2q)$ and AME$(11,2q)$ for every odd prime power $q\geq5$, AME$(13,2q)$ for $q\geq17$, AME$(15,2q)$ for $q\geq9$, and AME$(17,2q)$ for $q\geq67$. For every odd $N\geq3$, the same coupling gives AME$(N,2q)$ under the sufficient condition $q\geq\max\{N,2^{N-2}\}$ on the odd prime power $q$. Within this coupling, the smallest such $q$ must grow exponentially with $N$. Combined with known inputs and products, these families complete the nine-party classification: for integer $d\geq2$, an AME$(9,d)$ state exists if and only if $d\geq3$. Choosing the branch pairing also gives AME$(15,2p)$ states with a cyclic shift of the parties compensated by local unitaries, for every prime $p\equiv1\pmod{15}$.

item.title: Noise robust super-Heisenberg scaling in time-dependent quantum sensing by subspace-twirled dynamical decoupling
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that subspace‑twirled dynamical decoupling can preserve the signal of a time‑dependent Hamiltonian while canceling environmental noise, thereby delivering super‑Heisenberg scaling without the heavy overhead of adaptive control. By proving rigorous conditions under which the twirling protocol works, the authors bridge a gap between idealized quantum metrology proposals and realistic sensor hardware that must contend with decoherence. If experimentally realized, the technique could simplify the construction of ultraprecise magnetic or frequency sensors, although practical implementation will still need to verify the assumed noise models and control fidelity.

In quantum parameter estimation, time-dependent Hamiltonians can enable ultraprecise estimates of a physical parameter beyond the standard Heisenberg limit, also called the super-Heisenberg limit. However, achieving optimal scaling of the measurement precision typically requires an adaptive quantum control scheme which is resource-intensive and hard to implement in general. Furthermore, this advantage is often severely eroded by environmental noise. We propose the use of a dynamical decoupling scheme based on subspace twirling -- the averaging of random unitaries over a subspace rather than the entire Hilbert space -- to overcome these two limitations. We first prove necessary and sufficient conditions for subspace twirling to preserve the encoding signal while simultaneously removing environmental noise. We then establish conditions and provide performance guarantees for when time dependent Hamiltonians undergoing subspace twirling can achieve super-Heisenberg scaling without adaptive controls. Finally, we illustrate our results using an explicit example where a qubit sensor undergoing a subspace twirl simultaneously suppresses noise and achieves super-Heisenberg scaling. These results offer guidance for the design of ultraprecise quantum sensors under time-dependent and noisy conditions.

item.title: Entanglement detection from moments of the realigned state: application to continuous-variable quantum systems
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article introduces a practical entanglement‑witness that sidesteps full continuous‑variable tomography by measuring second‑order moments of the realigned density operator, an approach that can be implemented with a linear interferometer acting on multiple copies of the state. It builds directly on the recent multicopy techniques used to access partial‑transpose moments (Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033064 2026) and shows that even modest experimental resources suffice to certify entanglement in both Gaussian and highly non‑Gaussian states such as lossy NOON states. By providing a scalable, experimentally friendly tool, the work could accelerate verification of quantum‑optical platforms where full state reconstruction is prohibitive.

Certifying entanglement is a central problem in quantum information sciences, especially for continuous-variable quantum systems where full state tomography is experimentally demanding. We introduce a family of separability criteria based on the singular moments and weak moments of the operator obtained by applying the realignment map to the density operator. In practice, we find that the criterion based on the second-order moments of the realigned operator is already sufficient to witness the entanglement of a wide range of quantum optical states. The realigned moments can be readily accessed using an optical scheme consisting of a linear interferometer that couples several identical copies of the state, similarly to the multicopy technique used to measure the partial-transpose moments of a state [Phys. Rev. Research 8, 033064 (2026)]. We illustrate the detection capability of the second-order realigned-moment method for both Gaussian and non-Gaussian states, including lossy NOON states.

item.title: Communication Supremacy of a Qubit in Holevo Frenkel Weiner Scenario
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article overturns the long‑standing view that a lone qubit cannot outperform a classical bit in Holevo‑Frenkel‑Weiner communication tasks, showing that a carefully constrained six‑state preparation together with a three‑outcome measurement yields a provable quantum advantage even when no entanglement or other auxiliary resources are used. By introducing a robust witness that separates the achievable quantum strategies from any classical counterpart, the work not only clarifies the role of measurement incompatibility in communication supremacy but also provides a practical route to seedless certified randomness generation on modest hardware. The result dovetails with recent advances in device‑independent protocols and suggests that near‑term quantum networks could exploit single‑qubit channels for tasks previously thought to require richer resources, though experimental implementation will still need to manage the specific state‑preparation constraints and noise tolerances identified by the authors.

The prevailing wisdom asserts that in the Holevo Frenkel Weiner (HFW) framework of communication tasks, a qubit offers no advantage over a c bit unless additional quantum resources are supplied or the classical shared randomness (SR) is restricted. In contrast, we establish the supremacy of qubit communication in the HFW framework when additional quantum resources, such as entanglement or measurement incompatibility are not injected and SR is a free resource. We consider a prepare-measure scenario where the sender, Alice, prepares six states subject to a specific cryptographic constraint, and the receiver, Bob, performs a three-outcome measurement. Such a constraint on preparation impacts the power of qubit communication quite differently than that of c-bit communication, ultimately giving rise to the quantum advantage. We introduce a witness capable of distinguishing quantum strategies that lie beyond the set of possible classical strategies and demonstrate the optimal quantum advantage. {As an application, we demonstrate the generation of certified randomness without requiring any seed randomness, since Bob has no input.} We further analyse the robustness of the witness and show that the advantage persists in noisy situations, making it suitable for experimental realisation. Finally, we demonstrate that Bob's three outcome qubit positive operator valued-measure (POVMs) has a distinct capability of detecting coherence, which can be regarded as the non-classical feature responsible for showcasing the quantum advantage.

item.title: When can local unitaries generate a complete orthogonal basis?
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article settles a long‑standing open problem by proving that any pure state of two qutrits can be extended to a full orthogonal basis using only local unitary operations, establishing universal local encodability (ULE) for the $3\times3$ case and expanding the catalog of dimensions where ULE holds. By turning a heuristic parameter count into a rigorous necessary condition, the authors also identify infinitely many multipartite systems that can never be universally locally encoded, sharpening our understanding of which hardware architectures can support simple, fully local state‑preparation schemes. The operational link to measurement discrimination—showing that non‑ULE exactly corresponds to an advantage for general over projectively simulable measurements—provides a concrete benchmark for quantum sensing and verification protocols that rely on locally generated bases.

The question of local encodability asks: can a given, multipartite pure quantum state be completed to an orthonormal basis using only local unitary rotations? If any such state in a given system has this property, it is called universally locally encodable (ULE), a feature, which has applications in quantum information theory, engineering and math. Despite its easy formulation, the answer to this question depends nontrivially on the local dimensions of the system: While universal local encodability is known for $2\times 2$, $4\times 4$ and $8\times 8$-dimensional systems, it was so-far only conjectured to hold in $3\times 3$, and non-ULE was recently proved for systems of four and more qubits by Pauwels and Gühne. We resolve the open conjecture by proving universality for two qutrits. Furthermore, we construct (among others) universal local encodings in dimensions $d\times2$ for $d\ge2$, in dimensions $d\times3$ for $d=3,4$ and $d\ge6$, and in every bipartite system with one or two infinite-dimensional subsystems. For finite-dimensional multipartite systems, we turn a heuristic parameter count into a necessary condition for universality, which excludes universal local encodability in infinitely many cases. Finally, we give universal local encodability an operational interpretation by showing that non-ULE is equivalent to whether general measurements yield an advantage over projectively simulable ones in discrimination tasks where unknown, random local unitary rotations have to be detected.

item.title: Inter-city 18.9 km free-space QKD over a dense urban corridor
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows a major step toward real‑world deployment of free‑space quantum key distribution across cityscapes, achieving an 18.9 km link in dense Barcelona with modest hardware. By using room‑temperature detectors, no adaptive optics and a GPS‑disciplined synchronization scheme, the system delivers over 11 kbit/s of finite‑size secret key rate, demonstrating that high‑rate secure links are possible without exotic components and complementing recent fiber‑based network efforts. The work suggests metropolitan QKD could become a flexible add‑on to existing infrastructure, though its performance still depends on clear atmospheric conditions and line‑of‑sight geometry.

Terrestrial free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) provides a flexible complement to fiber-based networks, but its deployment over long horizontal paths in dense metropolitan environments remains challenging, as atmospheric turbulence, demanding pointing and tracking requirements, and operational constraints can substantially increase system complexity. We experimentally demonstrate the operation of a decoy-state BB84 system over an 18.9~km free-space link across a densely populated urban area in the metropolitan region of Barcelona using an aviation-compliant optical architecture. The system operates at 785~nm using room-temperature single-photon detectors and requires no adaptive optics at the receiver. The modular QKD transmitter, based on a deployment-oriented design, is interfaced with a versatile free-space optical terminal and an independent GPS-disciplined synchronization architecture, facilitating its integration into heterogeneous optical infrastructures. We present the transmitter performance and optical-link characteristics, together with a 40-minute field test characterized by an average channel attenuation of approximately 19~dB and a mean QBER of 1.31\%. From the measured channel parameters, we estimate an average finite-size secret key rate exceeding 11~kbit/s. These results demonstrate the feasibility of inter-city free-space QKD over dense urban areas using a comparatively simple architecture.

item.title: Reduced filtering using classical control hierarchy with linear optimality for continuous quantum error correction
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article demonstrates that continuous quantum error correction can be implemented with a dramatically smaller classical estimator—its exact filter scales with the syndrome space (dimension 3·2^{n‑k‑1}) rather than the full Hilbert space, making real‑time feedback far more tractable for near‑term devices. By exposing and correcting two subtle failure modes of the feedback loop, the authors raise entanglement fidelity in a three‑qubit code by nearly ten percent and provide a systematic gain‑design recipe that avoids controller stalling, linking directly to recent advances in autonomous and measurement‑based error correction. The results are most relevant for hardware platforms that can continuously monitor stabilizers, though they currently rely on a single Pauli recovery channel and full parity readout, so extending the approach to more general codes will be the next step.

Continuous quantum error correction promises reduced thresholds and hardware overhead compared to the digital paradigm, but its complex model estimation has greatly reduced its practicality. We recast this problem as a classical control-theoretic state hierarchy made of an exact bilinear reduced model, an exact conditional filter, and standard estimation and feedback design. For any $[[n,k,d]]$ stabilizer code whose generators are all continuously monitored and which is driven by a single Pauli recovery channel, we prove that the exact filter closes at dimension $3\cdot2^{\,n-k-1}$. This dimension is set by the syndrome space instead of the Hilbert space and is minimal within invariant-subspace filtering. The reduced model exposes and corrects two failure mechanisms of the feedback loop. Strong monitoring damps the rotational partner through which the controller steers the stabilizer and injects back-action diffusion along the recovery path; lowering the measurement strength during correction raises the entanglement fidelity of partner-steering LQR control by $0.096$ in the three-qubit code with three monitored parities. Linearizing at the codespace leaves the syndrome uncontrollable, so the controller can stall; a gain designed at a shifted operating point removes this degeneracy. In the limit of zero measurement during correction, we prove that a syndrome-only filter is exact at every recovery boundary. The resulting committed-recovery controller needs only $2^{\,n-k}$ class probabilities and gives the highest entanglement fidelity compared among the methods tested in the literature, $0.947$ against $0.920$ for a measurement-based estimator protocol in the three-qubit bit-flip code, and $0.726$ vs at most $0.407$ for continuous controllers in the five-qubit perfect code.

item.title: Residual Entanglement vs. Residual Coherence: A Wave Packet Approach in Neutrino Oscillation with Matter
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that treating neutrinos as wave packets rather than ideal plane waves fundamentally alters the predicted quantum‑correlation signatures—especially residual l₁‑norm coherence—along DUNE’s long baseline and beyond, highlighting how decoherence and matter effects can wash out oscillatory behavior. By expressing concurrence and three‑π entanglement directly in terms of measurable transition probabilities, the authors bridge high‑energy neutrino physics with quantum‑information tools, offering a new way to assess sensitivity to CP‑violating phases at very long distances. The work therefore provides theorists and experimentalists with realistic benchmarks for how coherence loss may limit future precision measurements, while also suggesting that residual coherence could become a novel observable in next‑generation neutrino experiments.

In this work, we investigate quantum correlations in three-flavor neutrino oscillations beyond the standard plane-wave (PW) description by employing a wave-packet formalism in the presence of constant matter density. We study three quantum correlation measures, namely the residual $l_1$-norm coherence, Concurrence Fill, and Three-$π$ entanglement, and express them in terms of transition probabilities for an initial muon-flavor state. The analysis is performed for the DUNE setup and extended beyond its baseline to study the interplay between wave-packet decoherence and matter effects over long distances. For the DUNE baseline, finite wave-packet widths suppress and smooth the oscillations relative to the PW case, with smaller widths causing stronger damping, while matter effects modify the amplitudes and positions of the oscillation features. Among the considered measures, residual $l_1$-norm coherence dominates over the entanglement measures. At very long propagation distances, wave-packet decoherence progressively washes out the oscillatory behavior, driving the oscillation probabilities and quantum correlation measures toward averaged values, with smaller wave-packet widths leading to earlier damping. Further, in the $L-δ_{\rm CP}$ plane, residual $l_1$-norm coherence exhibits weak $δ_{\rm CP}$ dependence, while Concurrence Fill and Three-$π$ entanglement show greater sensitivity at the DUNE baseline. Beyond a characteristic baseline in the extended propagation regime, all three measures approach constant values, independent of $L$ and $δ_{\rm CP}$.

item.description:

By achieving T1 and T2* comparable to existing Al/InAs gatemons and revealing a clear frequency‑dependent relaxation consistent with spontaneous emission, the work validates the ternary weak link as a viable building block for scalable hybrid circuits. The ability to tailor band structure and carrier density through Sb alloying opens new design space for higher‑frequency qubits and potentially better integration with semiconductor platforms, marking a concrete step toward more versatile superconducting‑semiconductor quantum processors.

Ternary InAsSb/Al nanowires combine compositionally engineerable semiconductor properties with epitaxial proximity superconductivity, making them attractive for hybrid quantum circuits and mesoscopic superconductivity. Here, we realize gatemon qubits based on shadow-defined in-situ InAsSb/Al Josephson junctions in a single growth process. Gate-dependent microwave spectroscopy demonstrates electrostatic tuning of the qubit transition over several gigahertz. Rabi oscillations and Ramsey interference show coherent qubit control, with representative values T1 = 0.79 us and T2* = 0.91 us. Across five gatemons distributed over three chips, the measured relaxation times range from approximately 0.2 us to 1 us and decrease with increasing qubit frequency. Their magnitude is comparable to a circuit estimate of spontaneous emission into the electromagnetic environment. These results establish in-situ InAsSb/Al junctions as coherent, gate-tunable circuit elements and introduce cQED architecture as a microwave probe of the dynamics of the ternary weak link.

item.title: Noise-Protected Superconducting Qudits from Higher-Harmonic Josephson Junctions
item.description:
Curator's Take: This article shows that the sign of the second‑harmonic term in a Josephson junction’s current–phase relation can be used as a design knob to create symmetry‑protected superconducting qutrits with dramatically reduced relaxation rates. By leveraging higher‑order harmonics—especially in emerging altermagnetic junctions—the work extends recent efforts to protect qubits (e.g., fluxonium and cat‑code devices) into the multi‑level regime, opening a path toward more compact hardware that stores more information per circuit element. The trade‑offs between exact charge selection rules and robustness against charge noise highlight practical material choices, while gate‑voltage–induced dephasing remains the primary hurdle to be engineered out.

Qudits, which generalize qubits to $d$ levels, store more information per circuit element than qubits. As with qubits, however, their sensitivity to noise must be overcome before they can be used for fault-tolerant quantum computing. Here we show that, by exploiting the second harmonic of the current--phase relation, a superconducting loop of three Josephson junctions can host qutrits strongly protected against relaxation, while dephasing limits their coherence. When the second harmonic is positive, a simple loop with a small asymmetry between the junctions provides a tunable, symmetry-protected qutrit. When it is negative, a protected qutrit can be realized by adding a small symmetry-breaking term, such as a weak Josephson diode effect. The two designs involve different trade-offs: the first has an exact charge selection rule, whereas the second is nearly insensitive to charge noise and its quasiparticle errors can be corrected. The preferable choice therefore depends on the materials used. Both require a sizable second harmonic to begin with, and we identify altermagnetic Josephson junctions as a candidate platform. Finally, microscopic calculations show that a gate voltage selects the sign of the second harmonic in these junctions, although gate-voltage noise then becomes the leading source of dephasing. These findings establish the sign of the second harmonic as a design principle for protected superconducting qudits.
